title: Latvian c.bank net  interventions  at zero last week
text:
RIGA, April 26 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Monday it had a zero net position for its currency interventions last week, down from a net 33 million euros ($44.36 million) the previous week.

On Monday, the lat <EURLVL=> continued to trade at the weaker end of its band against the euro and was quoted at a little firmer at 0.7069/79 euros compared with 0.7073/83 a week ago.

A zero position can mean that there was no trade or that the buying and selling of lats was balanced.

One trader said the market was stable and there were no significant changes expected as there was plenty of lats in the money markets.

The central bank automatically accepts offers to buy lats in what it calls passive intervention when the euro hits 0.7098 lats, the top end of its 1 percent fluctuation band based on a central rate of 0.7028.

Latvia took a 7.5 billion euro rescue package from the International Monetary Fund, the European Union and other donors at the end of 2008 to keep its currency stable.

Central bank interventions this year have been limited or even aimed at capping gains, cooling speculation the government would have to devalue the currency. (Reporting by Aija Braslina; Editing by Neil Stempleman)

title: Latvia  central bank  reserves up by 10 pct in March
text:
TALLINN, April 7 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Wednesday its foreign currency reserves rose by 9.94 percent in February to 5.57 billion euros ($7.44 billion) from 5.01 billion euros in the previous month as the third instalment of rescue package funds were paid to the government.

The Latvian lat has moved away from the weak end of its trading band to be close the same level last seen in December last year. The country is still awash with unplaced lats with banks not giving Lat denominated loans and so helping pull down yields on treasury bills, one of the few places to place lats.

The Latvian central bank said the increase in the reserves' was "mostly due to the third instalment of the loan received from the European Commission to the amount of 495.2 million euro."

The Latvian central bank added that it held convertible foreign currency of 5.228 billion euros up from 4.726 billion euros at the end of February.

Lithuania's official reserve assets were down by 15.3 percent month on month, or 2.99 billion litas ($1.16 billion) lower at 16.4 billion litas at the end of March.

The Lithuanian central bank said the central government's deposits contracted by 2.42 billion litas over the month.

Estonia's central bank's official reserve and foreign currency assets fell by 2.6 percent to 41.7 billion Estonian kroons ($3.56 billion) in March from 42.8 billion kroons at the end of February, the Estonian central bank said on its website on Wednesday.

title: Latvian c.bank net  interventions  at zero last week
text:
RIGA, March 29 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Monday it had a zero net position for interventions for the second week running last week, seen as a signal of easing pressure on the currency's band against the euro.

The lat's trading band come under pressure in 2008 and 2009 during an economic crisis that sent it to the IMF for help, but intervention this year has been limited or even aimed at capping gains, easing speculation the government would have to devalue.

In early trade, the lat <EURLVL=> was little changed from last week, with the euro quoted at 0.7074/84 lats compared with a 0.7075 close on Friday. The lat is still clear of the 0.7098 level at which the central bank intervenes.

However, one trader saw little chance the lat will appreciate further in its band.

"Banks have to make provisions for bad loans and therefore there is demand for euros," said one trader.

In Latvia, most loans are issued in euros and banks have to make provisions for bad loans, which have soared in the crisis, in that currency.

The central bank automatically accepts offers to buy lats in what it calls passive interventions when the euro hits 0.7098 lats, the top end of its 1 percent fluctuation band based on a central rate of 0.7028 lats.

The trader also noted that Latvian banks have started using a new central bank 7-day deposit facility, placing 397.2 million lats on March 26.

"That means that liquidity is still high and there is a surplus of lats in the market," said the trader.

The bank set an an interest rate of 1 percent on the facility, introduced to make liquidity more predictable.

Markets have remained calm in recent weeks despite the withdrawal of the largest party from the government, turning it into a minority administration.

(Reporting by Aija Braslina; editing by Patrick Graham)

title: Latvian c.bank says no net  interventions  last week
text:
RIGA, March 22 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Monday it ended last week with balanced net currency interventions and dealers said local markets remained calm despite political ups and downs.

The bank, which reports its currency interventions on a Monday for the previous week, made net purchases of 45 million euros two weeks ago.

In early trade, the lat <EURLVL=> was a touch weaker, with the euro quoted at 0.7072/87 lats after ending Friday at 0.7074/84, though it was still clear of the 0.7098 level at which the central bank intervenes.

"Events on the political stage have not affected the market as there are plenty of lats," said one trader.

Prime Minister Valdis Dombrovskis has been left with a minority government after the largest coalition party quit the government last week.

Dombrovskis is to hold talks this week with an opposition party as he seeks to rebuild his parliamentary majority.

The local financial market has taken the political shifts in its stride, banking that even if the opposition does not join the government it will not undermine Latvia's bailout programme with the International Monetary Fund and European Union.

Ratings agency Moody's said last week that Latvia had greater financial buffers now than a year ago and also that Dombrovskis did not face any big political decisions ahead of an Oct. 2 election that would be crucial for the bailout.

The trader said demand for euros could rise with the approach of the end of the month, when banks often tackle provisioning for bad loans, which has to be done in euros. This could drive the lat back up to intervention levels.

The central bank automatically accepts offers to buy lats in what it calls passive interventions when the euro hits 0.7098 lats, the top end of its 1 percent fluctuation band based on a central rate of 0.7028 lats. (Reporting by Aija Braslina, editing by Mike Peacock)

title: Latvia and Lithuanian c.bank reserves firm in Feb
text:
TALLINN, March 5 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Friday its foreign currency reserves rose by 3.18 percent in February to 5.07 billion euros ($6.89 billion) from 4.9 billion euros in the previous month after more rescue package funds was deposited in the country in the month.

Latvia's currency has remained close to the weak end of its trading band with the euro with the local money market awash with lats, but with limited opportunities for banks to invest in the local market and yields on t-bills fall to record lows.

The Latvian central bank said the increase in the reserves' was "mostly due to the third installment of the loan received from the International Monetary Fund for the amount of 200.26 million euro".

The Latvian central bank added that it held convertible foreign currency of 4.726 billion euros up from 4.484 billion euros at the end of January.

Lithuania's official reserve assets totaled 19.4 billion litas ($7.63 billion) at the end of February to show a 18 percent or 2.96 billion litas growth from the end of February.

Estonia's central bank's official reserve and foreign currency assets fell by 2.6 percent to 41.8 billion kroons ($3.63 billion) in February from a revised up amount of 42,9 billion kroons at the end of January, the Estonian central bank said on its website on Friday.

title: Latvia  central bank  reserves rise in Jan
text:
TALLINN, Feb 5 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Friday its foreign currency reserves rose by 2.2 percent in January to 4.9 billion euros ($6.72 billion) on the back of government deposits.

Latvia's currency has remained close to the weak end of its trading band with the euro with the local money market awash with lats, but with limited opportunies for banks to invest in the local market.

The bank said the increase in the reserves' was "due to the expansion of foreign currency funds deposits by the Latvian Government".

It added it held convertible foreign currency of 4.584 billion euros up from 4.484 billion euros at the end of December.

Latvia was the worst hit of the European Union's three small Baltic states in the financial crisis, forced to reach out to the IMF for support as it bid to keep its currency peg to the euro unchanged. Lithuania and Estonia have followed similar paths, although their decline has been less steep.

Lithuania's reserves rose by 2.8 percent from a month ago to 16.5 billion litas ($6.56 billion), the Lithuanian central bank also said on Friday.

Estonia's central bank reserves and foreign currency assets fell by 2.2 percent to 41.1 billion kroons ($3.60 billion) in January from the end of December, data on the Estonian central bank's website showed.

title: Latvia c.bnk reserves stable, Lithuania's fall in Dec
text:
RIGA, Jan 7 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Thursday its foreign currency reserves firmed 0.02 percent in December to 4.805 billion euros ($6.9 billion) from 4.804 billion euros in the previous month.

In late December Latvia's currency returned to the weak end of its trading band with the euro after companies squared their positions at the end of the year and an increase in end of month provision occurred.

The Latvian central bank said the small increase in the reserves' net position was due to the Latvian government depositing 31.83 million euros, while a decrease in domestic credit institutions foreign currency deposits reduced foreign currency reserves over the month.

The Latvian central bank added it held convertible foreign currency of 4.484 billion euros up from 4.479 billion euros at the end of November.

Lithuania's reserves fell by 12.4 percent from a month ago to 16 billion litas ($6.69 billion). The bank's reserves firmed by 1.4 percent at the end of 2009 compared to end of 2008, the Lithuanian central bank said also on Thursday.

The bank said its reserves contracted due to central government deposits falling by 2.4 billion litas and deposits of commercial banks were down by 0.3 billion.

Estonia's central bank's official reserve and foreign currency assets firmed to 43.3 billion kroons ($3.97 bln) in December from 41.7 billion kroons at the end of November, the Estonian central bank said on its website on Thursday.

Latvia announces its net position after its foreign exchange interventions every Monday, including on Reuters page <LVBANK11>. (Reporting by David Mardiste and Nerijus Adomaitis; Editing by Toby Chopra)

title: Latvia c.bank bought 19 mln euros last week
text:
RIGA, Jan 4 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Monday its foreign exchange interventions last week led to a net purchase of 19 million euros, down from net euro purchases of 45 million euros two weeks ago.

In early trade on Monday, the lat <EURLVL=> was slightly firmer, with the euro quoted at 0.7086/96 lats versus 0.7083/98 lats the Wednesday before the New Year holidays.

The central bank automatically accepts offers to buy lats in what it calls passive intervention when the euro hits 0.7098 lats, the top end of its 1 percent fluctuation band based on a central rate of 0.7028 lats.

"The positive position was due most likely to Latvian state treasury operations, as it must convert euros for lats via the central bank as part of the agreement with the IMF, while the market was opposite, with the lat at the weak end of its trading band," one trader said.

Traders expected a quiet week with little pressure on the lat and maybe some clients buying lats while it was weaker against the euro. They saw little speculative pressure.

The main cloud on the horizon is the hitch in talks with the International Monetary Fund and the European Union after a constitutional court ruling that plans to cut pensions were illegal.

This means the government needs to find a further 100 million lats in the budget this year, either from spending cuts, revenue rises or letting the budget deficit rise.

Any of these measures have to coordinated with the lenders, the government has said. Latvia at the end of 2008 struck a deal for a 7.5 billion euro international bailout, led by the IMF and EU and its fiscal policy has to be agreed with the lenders.

title: Latvia c.bank reserves rise, Lithuania's fall in Nov
text:
RIGA, Dec 7 (Reuters) - The Latvian central bank's foreign currency reserves rose 6.2 percent in November to 4.804 billion euros ($7.15 billion) from 4.523 billion euros in the previous month, it said on Monday.

For most of November, Latvia's currency was at the weak end of its band with the euro in thin trade on concerns that the country's 2010 budget cuts may not be approved by parliament and the IMF. By the end of the month, confidence and liquidity recovered with the currency firming slightly and the budget winning parliamentary approval.

The central bank said it held convertible foreign currency of 4.479 billion euros, up from 4.218 billion euros at the end of October.

Lithuania's reserves fell by 6.15 percent in November to 18.3 billion litas ($7.89 billion) from 19.5 million litas in October, the Lithuanian central bank said also on Monday.

The bank said its reserves shrank due to a fall of 937.9 million litas in central government deposits and a decrease of 388 million litas in Lithuania's external liabilities.

Estonia's foreign currency and gold reserves backing the Estonian kroon firmed by 8.0 percent in November to 40.4 billion kroons ($3.89 bln), up from 37.4 billion kroons at the end of October, its central bank said in a statement on Monday.

Latvia announces how much it has spent on passive interventions in the foreign exchange market every Monday, including on Reuters page <LVBANK11>. In the last week, the Latvian central bank bought 105 million euros and sold lats. (Reporting by David Mardiste; Editing by Victoria Main)

title: Latvia  lat steady, cbank did not  intervene  last wk
text:
RIGA, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Monday it did not make any foreign exchange interventions for the second week running last week with liquidity up and fewer worries over the passing the 2010 budget on Tuesday.

In early trade on Monday, the lat <EURLVL=> was slightly weaker, but still below the central bank's intervention level at 0.7080/95 lats compared to 0.7081/91 lats last Monday.

"The situation in the market is calm with a surplus of short-term money and there is the expectation that the 2010 budget's second reading tomorrow will not be a problem," one trader said.

Traders said the government appears to have accepted what it must do for the budget and although they do not like it, the government understands that it will have to pass the budget to keep the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and international lenders on side to support a 7.5 billion euro ($11.3 bln) rescue package the country needs.

In the week before last, the central bank also said that it made no interventions in the currency market, and earlier in November the only trade the central bank was doing was converting funds for the government treasury's requirements as required by their agreement with the IMF.

Liquidity has improved over the last two last weeks with yields on Latvia's domestic borrowing falling by more than one percent and with more participants bidding making the weekly auctions heavily over-subscribed.

The central bank automatically accepts offers to buy lats when the euro hits 0.7098 lats, the top end of its 1 percent fluctuation band based on a central rate of 0.7028 lats.

Latvia relies on 7.5 billion euro international monetary fund (IMF) rescue package to keep its finances afloat, but the country's fiscal policy must meet IMF and European Commission approval before more payments from the loan are disbursed.

The central bank announces interventions on Monday for the previous week, including on the <LVBANK11> Reuters page. title: Latvia  FX  reserves ease, Lithuania's up in Oct
text:
RIGA, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Friday its foreign currency reserves fell 1.2 percent in October, while Lithuania's central bank said its reserves grew sharply.

Latvia's currency has been trading at the weak end of its band with the euro in recent weeks on concerns the International Monetary Fund may not approve the government's 2010 budget cuts and on the risk of political instability.

Its central bank said reserves slipped to 4.523 billion euros ($6.82 billion) from 4.577 billion euros in September. It said it held convertible foreign currency of 4.218 billion euros, slightly down from 4.277 billion euros at the end of September.

Lithuania's reserves increased by 22.7 percent in October to 19.5 billion litas ($8.37 billion) from 15.9 million litas in September, its central bank said on Friday.

The bank said the reserves were boosted by the central government's deposit of 2.7 billion litas after a successful bond issue during the month.

Estonia's foreign currency and gold reserves backing the Estonian kroon eased just 0.1 percent in October to 37.4 billion kroons ($3.55 bln), down from 37.39 billion kroons at the end of September, the Estonian central bank said in a statement on Friday.

title: Latvia  currency  dips, eyes on budget, govt tensions
text:
RIGA, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Latvia's lat weakened again to the central bank's intervention level on Friday with the market remaining focussed on the coalition government's efforts to draw up the 2010 budget and any signs of further political tensions.

 One trader said the suspension on Thursday of the head of the tax office by the finance minister, portrayed in Latvian media as a source of tension within the ruling coalition or even a reason for it to fall, could show up eventually in longer-term lending rates.

 The euro <EURLVL=> was last quoted at 0.7078/98 lats after being earlier at 0.7082/97 lats. The central bank automatically takes offers to buy lats when the euro reaches 0.7098 lats in what it calls passive intervention.

 "There is not much more activity than usual (in the spot forex market). Most money market activity is still in the week and month duration due to continued uncertainty," said another dealer.

 He said the uncertainty came from the government's drawing up of the 2010 budget and whether it would be enough to meet the terms of the international rescue programme as well as from the political situation within the ruling coalition.

 The clash between Finance Minister Einars Repse and Tax Office chief Dzintars Jakans has been brewing for weeks and Repse on Thursday suspended Jakans.

 Latvian media speculated that this could lead to tensions between the New Era party to which Repse belongs and the largest coalition party, the People's Party.

 However, People's Party chairman, and the justice minister, Marek Seglins, played down such an idea.

 Asked during a morning radio interview whether the tax office clash would lead to the falling of the government, Seglins said: "I don't think so...I hope not."

 He said now was a time of great responsibility and the finance minister should focus on the 2010 budget.  (Reporting by Patrick Lannin; editing by Patrick Graham)

title: UPDATE 1-Swedbank says mortgage plan threatens Latvia ops
text:
* Would review Latvian operation if mortgage plan passed

* Banks to meet Latvian prime minister next week

* Swedbank has $3.4 bln exposure to Latvian mortgage market

* Swedbank shares rise on Nordea merger speculation

(Adds quotes from Latvian commercial bank association)

STOCKHOLM/RIGA, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Swedbank said on Monday it would review its business in Latvia if a controversial mortgage plan went through, and banks said they would meet the country's prime minister next week to discuss the issue.

Latvia's Prime Minister, Valdis Dombrovskis, angered banks last week with his surprise proposal. [ID:nL8188838]

He said he wanted to limit what banks can collect from defaulted home loan takers to the collateral, which would cause banks' bad debt losses to soar as many property values have slumped below the value of the debts used to purchase them.

"If this runs through we need to reconsider our operations in Latvia," said Thomas Backteman, vice president of corporate communications for Swedbank, the largest bank in Latvia and the one most exposed to the harsh recession in the Baltic states.

He said he did not believe the proposal would fly, but that the bank was closely monitoring the situation.

Passing the proposal would increase political risk and make it difficult to work in a situation when a government decides legal issues retroactively. "That's very far from the established legal practice in the EU," he said.

He said banks would meet the prime minister on Oct. 22.

This was seconded by the head of the Association of Latvian Commercial Banks.

"We will give our arguments that this idea is absurd and without any base and is against Latvian civil law," association head Teodors Tverijons told Reuters. If it was carried out, it would lead to sharp reductions in crediting from banks.

The banks would also meet European Economic and Monetary Affairs Commissioner Joaquin Almunia, who is visiting Latvia on Tuesday to push Latvia to live up to promises to slash its 2010 budget deficit. "We cannot keep quiet about this," he said.

Though Latvia's woes have overshadowed Swedbank recently, its shares got a lift after a report that a possible tie up with largest Nordic bank Nordea could be in the pipes.

by 1426 GMT, Swedbank shares were up 5.5 percent. "It's partly the rumours about a merger with Nordea and the fact the bank is threatening to downsize in Latvia," said a trader.

Swedish daily Dagens Nyheter said a possible merger between Swedbank and Nordea was being evaluated by Nordea's largest shareholder, Sampo.

Sampo and Swedbank declined to comment on the matter.

EXPOSURE

Analysts have said the reform would effectively mean people could walk away from their debts and leave their properties in the hands of the bank.

Some analysts have also seen a devaluation risk in the proposal as it would cap home owners' losses, most of whom have loans in foreign currencies. Dombrovskis has denied any link with devaluation in his proposal. Latvia's central bank continued to intervene in the foreign exchange market last week. It said on Monday it sold 15 million euros and bought lats amid controversy over the country's 2010 budget plans. [ID:nC2041]

The lat was slightly firmer in late trade after the government earlier promised to make the budget adjustments that international lenders want it to carry out.

Backteman said Swedbank had a "substantial" exposure to the Latvian mortgage market. Out of a total of some 61 billion crowns ($8.7 billion) of exposure to Latvia, 24 billion crowns came from mortgage loans, he said.

Latvia's bank sector is led by Swedbank , SEB , Nordea and DNB Nord , which are already facing big losses in a real estate crash.

Nordea said its total lending in Latvia is about 3.1 billion euros ($4.56 billion), of which 1.1 billion was housing loans.

SEB said the impact on it was restricted as lending in Latvia was 3 percent of total loans to corporates and homes.

It said lending to corporates and households in Latvia was 40 billion crowns, of which 11 billion crowns was mortgages. SEB said it was also planning to participate in the meeting next week. (Additional reporting by Brett Young in Helsinki; Editing by John Stonestreet and Andrew Macdonald) ($1=7.037 Swedish Crown) ($1=.6795 Euro)

title: UPDATE 1-Latvian lat fears back in focus on loan wrangles
text:
* Latvia lat at c.bank intervention level, volumes low

* Baltic state back in focus due budget, loan wrangles

* Fitch affirms rating, sees downgrade if IMF/EU programme

unravels

* Latvian prime minister criticises Swedish finance minister

as aggressive, plays down budget worries (Adds analysts, Fitch, prime minister)

By Patrick Lannin

RIGA, Oct 6 (Reuters) - The Latvian lat fell to the weak end of its pegged band against the euro on Tuesday after worries over devaluation and hitches in talks with international lenders re-emerged, dealers said.

However, analysts disagreed about devaluation chances and the extent of the budget worries and the prime minister was quoted as reiterating he thought his country was making enough of an effort to meet the terms of its 7.5 billion euro rescue.

By 1301 GMT, the euro <EURLVL=> was quoted at 0.7078/98 lats, the top end of the central bank's 1 percent fluctuation band of the euro against the lat. Overnight rates <LVLF=> remained low, though, at 0.50/1.10 percent.

"All the comments from Sweden/IMF/EU have led to more pressure. Euro and lat spot is firmly on the top now and all the customers are getting more and more worried," said one trader.

Another said that with the lat just sitting at the top of the band, rather than going through it, the central bank might not have to carry out what it calls its passive interventions.

The lat is pegged to the euro at a central rate of 0.7028 lats, with a 1 percent fluctuation band.

Latvia has strongly rejected any idea it should devalue and said this would not help its economic recovery. But some economists see it likely if Latvia hits problems with lenders.

"I still wouldn't rule out the possibility of Latvia being pushed into some forced currency adjustment. I'm not sure if it wil be a whole-hearted devaluation or a depegging," said RBC strategist Nigel Rendall.

He said Latvia's proposed budget cuts to meet 2010 budget goals under the 7.5 billion euro rescue led by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and European Union (EU) were not enough as new revenues would not be able to fill the funding gap.

But Nordea Markets analyst Annika Lindbald wrote in a note that worries about Latvia were overdone, though she also expected more cliff hanger talks with lenders.

She said concerns about an imminent collapse "also appear greatly exaggerated" as Latvia was well funded after recent IMF and EU loan disbursements.

"Unfortunately Latvia might need to move closer to the prospect of state insolvency again for the 500 million lats of fiscal consolidation measures to be approved," she added.

"AGGRESSIVE" SWEDEN

The government of Prime Minister Valdis Dombrovskis plans spending cuts of just 225 million lats ($463.6 million), leading to doubts it will meet a promised 500 million lat deficit cut.

The government says the planned cuts, some tax rises and carry through from 2009 reductions, will meet the deficit goal.

But Swedish Finance Minister Anders Borg, whose government put funds in the rescue deal due to Swedish bank exposure, said at the weekend international patience with Latvia was limited.

Dombrovskis, in an interview to Swedish business daily Dagens Industri, hit back. "I have had discussions with the European Commission and IMF representatives and none of them were as aggressive as Mr Borg," he told the newspaper.

He also reiterated that currently planned fiscal measures were enough to reach the goals of the loan programme.

Ratings agency Fitch affirmed its current BB+ rating on Latvia with a negative outlook, but raised a warning flag.

"Failure to implement budget cuts and remain on track with the EU/IMF programme could lead to a downgrade," it said.

"A delay to the disbursement of international funds to Latvia would leave fiscal and external financing gaps, undermine confidence and put renewed pressure on the exchange rate." (Reporting by Patrick Lannin; editing by Chris Pizzey)

The devaluation fears surrounding the small Baltic state have spilled over into other markets.

Interbank market rates, which have also soared to record levels in response to the jitters, were quoted Monday morning at 14.80/19.60 percent.

title: UPDATE 5-Latvians agree budget cuts, eye EU/IMF aid
text:
* Latvian PM says agreement on budget cuts reached

* S&P puts Latvia credit rating on negative watch

* Swedish bank shares and crown surge

* Latvian currency hits four-month high against euro

(Adds EU quotes)

By Laura MacInnis and Patrick Lannin

RIGA, June 8 (Reuters) - Latvia's government and coalition partners agreed on Monday to slash the country's 2009 budget, a move that could help it secure more emergency loan funds and stave off pressure to devalue its currency.

News of the deal to cut 500 million lats ($978.9 million) in public spending caused a jump in the Swedish crown and Swedish banks, whose exposure to the Baltics has raised fears that a Latvian meltdown could have effects across the region.

Shares in Swedbank traded 8 percent higher and SEB was up nearly 9 percent in late-afternoon trade.

But in a sign that nervousness about Latvia remained, ratings agency Standard & Poor's placed Latvia's "BB-plus" long-term rating, which is already at junk level, on "CreditWatch" with negative implications.

Joaquin Almunia, European economic and monetary affairs commissioner, said the next instalment of aid to Latvia would depend on fiscal cuts. [ID:nL7175766]

"We are trying to support their efforts and we are ready to adopt the next instalment of our financial support provided the reforms needed and the adjustment needed will be adopted by their government and their parliament," he said after a meeting of Eurogroup finance ministers.

He said they had not discussed Latvia but a senior Eurogroup source said they had.

Latvian Prime Minister Valdis Dombrovskis told journalists that a meeting of government coalition parties, the president, social partners and central bank had agreed on 500 million lats of cuts which would be put into a second reading of the budget.

The government said in a statement it would hold a meeting on Tuesday on the budget cuts.

The Latvian government will meet on Tuesday to discuss the details of the budget cuts agreed to in principle on Monday, and to chart the way forward for the country that faces a near 20 percent shrinkage of its economy this year.

Worries about the drop in the economy have led to fears of a devaluation, which caused jitters in other markets last week.

But given a wave of central bank intervention, which has drained the local currency market of liquidity and caused interbank rates to soar, the lat firmed to a four-month high against the euro. <EURLVL=>

Investors have been concerned Latvia might not win access to the next instalment of its 7.5 billion euro ($10.4 billion) International Monetary Fund and European Union rescue loan, but one analyst said the jury would still be out on the lat even if further funding was agreed.

"We believe that (an IMF deal) is going to give some sort of indication of the future, but before that matter is resolved we are not able to make a judgment (about market conditions)," said Annika Lindblad, a Baltic analyst at Nordea bank.

S&P said its decision to place Latvia on credit watch, which could lead to a further downgrade in its long-term rating, was due to increased pressure on the sovereign's currency in the near term.

"Despite continued government efforts to contain the fiscal deficit and ensure the inflow of funds from multilateral lenders, we believe the likelihood of a currency adjustment in the next few months has substantially increased," S&P said.

Latvian officials have repeatedly said they will not devalue. The prime minister of neighbouring Estonia, Andrus Ansip, said in Stockholm: "I don't think that the Latvian lat will be devalued," adding this would only create more problems.

LAT GAINS

Dropping the currency peg would set back Latvia's goal of joining the euro zone and also inflict pain on its companies and citizens holding foreign-denominated loans.

It may also hurt the currencies of neighbours Estonia and Lithuania, though Ansip said he did not see this as the case.

Latvia's central bank said foreign exchange interventions rose last week to a new 2009 high of 237.3 million euros.

The interventions and tight money market helped the lat to firm, with the euro being quoted at 0.7050/60 lats by 1525 GMT.

The central bank, which has spent 907 million euros this year on propping up the lat, manages it within a 1 percent fluctuation band. The intervention benchmark is at 0.7098 lats.

Neil Shearing, an emerging Europe specialist at Capital Economics, said the lat strength did not negate concerns about Latvia, whose wages and asset prices soared during the global economic boom and then crashed when recession set in.

"They would benefit from a weaker exchange rate, and they may need one," he said, also cautioning after the statistics office reported Latvian consumer prices fell 0.5 percent in May that deflation must be carefully watched to avoid future damage.

"The bigger picture is that a number of countries have gone down this route of trying to adjust their exchange rate through prices and lower wages ... and basically failed," Shearing said, pointing to Venezuela and Peru in the mid-1980s as examples. (Editing by Stephen Nisbet and Dale Hudson)

title: UPDATE 2-Latvian mkts stay nervy, eyes on budget and IMF
text:
(Adds European Commission statement, treasury intervention)

RIGA/LONDON, June 4 (Reuters) - Latvia's lat hit an almost 3-month high against the euro on Thursday, boosted by reports of government buying and speculation that support from international bodies might help fend off a currency devaluation.

Bank-to-bank interest rates in the small Baltic state rose to a record 25 percent, however, and nerves are still strained over the prospect of a cut in the lat's value that would hammer Swedish banks and reignite concerns over the fate of eastern Europe in the global financial crisis.

A failed government debt sale on Wednesday added to the surge in interbank lending costs and comments from Swedish and other officials this week, intensifying speculation that devaluing is the only way to cure its collapsing economy.

But Latvia's leaders have stood firm behind the peg for months, even as the economy shrank by a fifth year-on-year, and on Thursday there was no sign of them backing down.

"The Bank of Latvia has chosen a certain policy, defining it and explaining to society and is carrying it out," the central bank said in a statement.

"The Bank of Latvia has explained the negative effect of a devaluation on people, companies and the solvency of the state."

The lat firmed away from central bank intervention levels with dealers citing purchases of lats by the Treasury.

By 1020 GMT, the euro <EURLVL=> was quoted at 0.7070/80 lats, well away from the 0.7098 level at which the central bank intervenes to keep the lat within a 1 percent fluctuation band to the euro.

"The reason for the rise is that first of all the market is quite tight and the state treasury has also been doing some euro-lat trades," said one trader.

The treasury had no immediate comment.

BUDGET KEY

Prime Minister Valdis Dombrovskis said on Wednesday he must reach a deal swiftly on the release of more IMF and EU funds under last year's 7.5 billion euro ($10.72 billion) bailout, in the hope that will calm nerves around the country's finances.

A payout has been linked to further cuts in spending to account for a worsening economic picture and the 2009 budget faces a first reading in parliament on Thursday, with other cuts still being discussed.

"European Economic and Monetary Affairs Commissioner Joaquin Almunia believes that the new budgetary proposals are a step in the right direction and also appear to contain some welcome reforms," the European Commission said in a statement.

"But more is needed to contain the increase in the budget deficit."

The Commission said the International Monetary Fund (IMF), whcih led the pair's bailout of Latvia last year, would also make a statements on work on the 2009 budget.

Liquidity in the currency market has been strained by the central bank buying lats to keep the currency within its one percent band against the euro.

Overnight deposit rates were bid as high as 25 percent <LVLOND=>, Reuters charts indicated, up from the previous day's peak of 24 percent.

Given the high overnight rates, the euro fell to 0.7084/94 lats, away from the level at which the central bank intervenes to support it, though it later edged back again to 0.7088/98, with 0.7098 euros being the intervention level.

One money market trader said lat liquidity might ease in the coming days as banks had borrowed more money from the central bank on Wednesday than the previous day.

Data from the central bank <LVBANK11> showed that on Wednesday banks borrowed a total 213.2 million lats ($426.5 million) from the central bank, mostly via the marginal lending facility. This was up from 119.8 million lats on Tuesday. (Reporting by Patrick Lannin, Jamie McGeever and Marcin Grajewski, writing by Patrick Graham)

title: UPDATE 1-Latvia c.bank supports lat, rejects devaluation
text:
(Adds central bank chief quotes from newspaper)

Ilmars Rimsevics said lowering the value of the lat would lead to inflation, a long delay in introducing the euro and a fall in trust in Latvia.

Instead, the government had to pursue budget cutting plans to win further lending from the IMF and EU.

"A devaluation would lead to the end for many years of the dream of adopting the euro in 2012 or at the latest in 2013," Rimsevics wrote in the Latvijas Avize daily newspaper.

Rimsevics was replying to an article last week by a former prime minister, who called for a 30 percent devaluation in order to boost exports and help Latvia out of its crisis.

Fears of a lat devaluation affected markets last week, sending down the Swedish crown and Swedish bank shares due to worries about the Nordic state's exposure to the Baltic region.

Rimsevics said supporters of devaluation also favoured paying taxes in euros and a one-sided introduction of the euro, without waiting for formal entry into the currency union.

"That would lead to an even greater loss of trust to the national currency, the lat, to greater international isolation," he wrote. To avoid this, the government had to stick to its path of cutting spending and get more IMF and EU loans budget.

title: UPDATE:  Latvia  Ctrl Bk: Forex Intervention  Over For Time Being
text:
LONDON (Dow Jones)--Latvia's latest round of foreign exchange intervention is over "for the time being," Bank of Latvia Monetary Policy Head Karlis Bauze said Friday.

"During the previous two weeks we did intervene," Bauze said, adding that the intervention was over "for the time being," after an investment of around EUR170 million designed to defend the currency's euro peg.

The Latvian currency is fixed at a central parity of 0.702804 and allowed by the central bank to fluctuate plus or minus 1%.

Bauze said the Latvian central bank would have to revise down its current growth forecasts on the financial market turmoil.

"We do those forecasts twice a year," he said. "There will be revisions made particularly in line with the current market conditions."

The Bank of Latvia currently predicts gross domestic product growth of 0.5% on the year in 2008, 1.0% on the year in 2009 and 3.1% on the year in 2010, well below the double digit growth recorded in 2007.

"We are looking vigilantly at what's happening in the financial markets," the central banker said. "We are in turbulent times."

But he said current investor appetite for risk wasn't affecting Latvia's ability to borrow.

"At the moment the government doesn't need to borrow as it can get investment from the European Investment Bank," Bauze said. Because of this, "risk adverseness is not directly affecting the government's ability to borrow," he said.

And he said he thought Latvia's current account deficit will unwind gradually, narrowing to below 10% of gross domestic product in 2009.

Latvia's current account deficit was 15.6% of the country's GDP in the second quarter, sparking concerns that the Baltic country would be vulnerable to tight credit markets resulting from the recent financial turmoil, as it borrowed to finance growth.

But Bauze said he expected the "external imbalances to unwind gradually."

Speaking at an investment event, he said the current account deficit would "diminish gradually" and "fall below 10% in 2009".

title: UPDATE 2- Latvia  c.bank chief says to keep  intervening
text:
(Adds central bank quotes)   

RIGA, March 28 (Reuters) - Latvian central bank chief Ilmars Rimsevics said on Wednesday the bank would keep intervening to support the lat currency, which has been stuck at the lower end of its band against the euro since mid-February.   

"A devaluation would not be the cure, it would be the poison," Rimsevics told a news conference, repeating earlier assurances that the bank had no plans devalue the lat.   

"As long as the current account deficit is supported by long-term finances there is no risk to the lat," he added.   

The bank had given no thought to widening the euro trade band of the lat, now set at plus or minus 1 percent around a central rate.   

"We are more than happy to intervene whenever it is necessary and we will continue to intervene for as long as it is necessary," Rimsevics said. He was speaking to journalists after a debate on the economy at a local university.   

Baltic news agency BSN also quoted Rimsevics as saying that credit growth, one of the causes of strong economic expansion, would slow.   

"If in 2006 credit growth was 60 percent then this year we hope that it will grow by 40 percent," he said.   

He said the authorities had to continue to reassure foreign investors and banks so that they would not quit Latvia and to ensure a stable macroeconomic climate, BNS quoted him saying.   

The lat, over which the bank last week spent 195 million euros in support, was quoted at 0.7096/01 to the euro by 1220 GMT.   

Danske Bank analyst Lars Christensen said he wanted to see a strong action plan from the government to fight inflation and the other imbalances which have got some investors worried and helped keep the lat at the lower end of its band.   

"The central bank chief is saying he will intervene as long as needed. But he can intervene only as long as he has the FX reserves and he has used up almost 10 percent of his reserves in two weeks," Christensen added.   

Rimsevics has said that the central bank has 2.5 billion Latvian lats ($4.71 billion) of reserves.   

"What I want to see is a strong policy statement from the government announcing measures to counter this situation. The measures have to be large, significant and credible, unlike the ones they announced a few weeks back," Christensen added.   

The government recently announced a plan to fight inflation, involving moving to a balanced budget and then a surplus faster than planned. (additional reporting by Sujata Rao in London)

title: WRAPUP 1- Latvia  c.bank says may keep  intervening  to back lat
text:
RIGA, March 26 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Monday it may have to keep up "passive" intervention efforts to support the lat after selling nearly 200 million euros last week.   

Surging inflation, fears of economic overheating and rumours of a devaluation have pushed the lat to the bottom end of its permitted trading range against the euro in recent weeks.   

On the sidelines of a meeting of euro zone finance ministers in Brussels, Eurogroup Chairman Jean-Claude Juncker said European Union finance chiefs should discuss "all recent developments in the Latvian context".   

Latvia's central bank <LVBANK11> said on Monday it sold a net 195.5 million euros in "passive" intervention between March 19 and 25 to support the lat, up from 65 million the prior week.   

"I would not be surprised if the central bank will have to keep intervening for some time, but we are more than happy to do so,"  Bank of Latvia spokesman Martins Gravitis told Reuters.   

The central bank began intervening in currency markets this month for the first time since 2001.   

The lat was quoted at 0.7093 at 1600 GMT <EURLVL=> on Monday versus its lowest permitted rate of 0.7098.   

Worries about supercharged growth and rising prices led  Standard & Poor's on Feb. 19 to lower its outlook for Latvia to negative from stable.   

Rating agencies have also cited a large current account deficit -- 21 percent of gross domestic product last year -- and strong consumption as signs the economy is growing too fast.   

Fitch warned on March 6 that all three Baltic states were in danger of overheating, though it said Latvia faced the biggest risk of a hard landing.   

Latvia's gross domestic product grew a record 11.9 percent in 2006 and inflation in February was 7.3 percent, up from 7.1 percent the previous month.   

In an effort to rein in growth and inflation, the  Bank of Latvia on March 15 raised its key interest rate by 50 basis points to 5.5 percent. The government also has announced a proposal to tighten fiscal policy and curb credit growth.   

Valery Kargin president of  Parex Bank, Latvia's second biggest by deposits, told Reuters he had little faith in the government's planned measures.   

"I don't think the government's inflation action plan will help to reduce inflation," he said, adding that he held the central bank responsible for negative sentiment about the lat.   

However, he said he did not think "there will be any devaluation of the lat".   

Swift growth and price pressures have dashed Latvia's hopes of joining the euro next year and central bank chief Ilmars Rimsevics told Reuters last week 2012 was "the most realistic date" for Latvia to join the euro.   

The lat is pegged to the euro under a currency board-type system with a central rate of 0.702804 to the single currency.   

Since April 2005, it has been in the ERM-2 exchange rate mechanism, where the permitted fluctuation band is +/- 15 percent around the agreed central rate. Latvia has unilaterally set a 1 percent fluctuation band.

title: INTERVIEW-C.bank chief sees soft landing in Latvia
text:
RIGA, March 20 (Reuters) - The head of Latvia's central bank said on Tuesday that he expected a soft landing of the economy and warned that anyone speculating against the lat currency would get their fingers burnt.  

In an interview, Ilmars Rimsevics said some of the recent comments about his small Baltic nation showed a lack of understanding about its economy, and some writers appeared not even to know where it was.  

Latvia has attracted much attention in recent weeks, sparked by a devaluation rumour that swept the country in mid-February. The lat has since then been stuck at the lowest end of its range, near 0.7098 to the euro <EURLVL=>.  

But Rimsevics told Reuters: "It is difficult, it is challenging, it is not a crisis."  

Ratings agencies have warned about Latvia's high inflation, more than 7 percent so far this year, and have pointed to a large current account deficit, of more than 20 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).  

The central bank recently raised a key interest rate, the refinancing rate, to 5.5 percent from 5.0 percent and last week spent 65 million euros to buy lats on the market.  

"If you interview any economist or central banker I think there will be very few who would as a first option mention a hard landing. I definitely believe that we will have a soft landing," Rimsevics said.  

He said some people wanted to speculate against the lat, which is fixed to the euro and is in the ERM-2 grid.  

Such speculation had happened during a bank crisis in 1995 and in the emerging markets meltdown three years later, he said.  

"Of course they burnt their fingers in '95, they burnt their fingers in '98 and they will burn their fingers in 2007," said Rimsevics, who has been at the bank 15 years and has been its head since 2001.  

"The currency will not be devalued, which is what they are betting on," he said. Some speculators still had positions in the lat, he added.  

He also hit out at some analysts and commentators, who he said had shown a lack of knowledge about the region.  

"When we have seen some articles where Latvia has been described as a country from the Balkans, then that gives me the right and also the chance to say that some people don't even know where Latvia is," he said.  

GOVERNMENT INFLATION PLAN  

Rimsevics shared some of the concerns expressed by the ratings agencies, but said the economy was "getting first aid".  

He cited the government's recently launched plan to bring down inflation, which includes the fiscal tightening of moving the budget to balance this year and next and then to surplus.  

New real estate deal taxes will also be introduced to cool the property market, where prices have soared amid strong lending growth by the banks.  

He said the government's action plan was lacking in some respects, but overall he thought it was credible.  

"It is maybe a little bit delayed, but if carried out properly, without any hesitation, first of all on the fiscal front, it will reach the numbers envisaged," he said.  

Rimsevics indicated there was not much the bank itself could do on monetary policy, even if it raised rates last week.  

He said this served more as a signal of concern about inflation rather than a practical instrument as banks did not really use the refinancing rate.  

The government expects inflation to fall to 2.0 to 2.5 percent by 2011. Rimsevics said this indicated "that 2012 is the most realistic date when Latvia could introduce the euro".  

He also said central bank interventions to support the lat should be seen in the context of purchases of 1 billion euros last year to stop the lat appreciating to the top of its band.

STOCKHOLM, March 19 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Monday it sold 65 million euros last week in "passive" intervention to support the lat which remained weak because local banks were rebuilding stocks of foreign currency.  

Central bank data <LVBANK11> on Monday showed the bank made the sales between March 12 and 18 in its first intervention since 2001, but a bank spokesman said there was no follow-up action on Monday.  

A central bank official said the lat remained weak because domestic banks were rebuilding euro positions depleted after devaluations rumours in mid-February and as foreign bank hedging caused a sharp rise in demand for foreign currency.  

"The Latvian central bank has not been on the market today," said spokesman Martinsh Gravitis.  

The central bank intervened on Thursday and Friday to support the currency, which has sunk to stay near or at the weakest permitted rate of 0.7098 to the euro in its fluctuation band of 1 percent around a central rate.  

The devaluation rumours began to spread on Feb. 16 via mobile phone messages, sending people flocking to currency exchange booths to buy euros and dollars.  

In passive intervention, commercial banks can sell the central bank euros when the lat reaches the lower end of its band, but the central bank does not go into the market.  

The lat was quoted at around 0.7095 to the euro on Monday, still pinned at the weak end of its fluctuation range.  

Latvian central bank chief economist Uldis Rutkaste, speaking at a conference on the Baltic state's economy in the Swedish capital, said the lat's continued weakness "largely reflects the fact that domestic banks are trying to rebuild their euro position."  

He told Reuters after the seminar that banks had to rebuild stocks after selling foreign exchange to meet residents' demand for euros on the devaluation rumour, and then as foreign banks had hedged their lat positions.  

He described the central bank intervention as small scale.  

The central bank and the government have strongly denied any plan to devalue the currency.  

Rutkaste said that one of the reasons for Latvia's consumer-led economic boom had been flows of funds to local banks from their foreign parents, Swedish banks SEB and Swedbank.  

"The Bank of Latvia's position is that foreign inflows are too high. The domestic economy cannot absorb such high flows," he added.  

The bank would be more comfortable if economic growth was 7 to 8 percent rather than the more than 11 percent of 2006.  

Swedbank chief executive Jan Liden told the conference that he expected a much lower growth of credit volumes this year.

title: Latvia  lat retreats further from  intervention  level.
text:
RIGA, Jan 10 (Reuters) - The Latvian lat eased thurther on Thursday as a narrowing rate differential between the lat and SDR currencies make the local unit less attractive for speculation, dealers said. 

 At 1059 GMT, the lat was 26 points off the strongest level the central bank allows it to hit, after trading 21 points off the intervention level near close on Wednesday. 

 "The lat is not as attractive any more since the rates are falling and consequently there is no such a strong demand for lats," said Girts Polis, forex dealer at Nordea's Latvian arm. 

 A wide rate differential between the lat and SDR currencies pushed funds into the local unit in the last months of 2001, bringing the lat to the top of its trading band. 

 On Thursday, average one-year interbank rate stood at 5.00/6.00 percent, down from 5.83/6.83 percent a month ago, and they have a tendency to decline. 

 On the local forex market the dollar was 0.6319/24 against the lat compared to the central bank's rate of 0.6293/420, where it intervenes to keep the currency within its allowed range. 

 The lat is pegged at 0.7997 to the IMF's world currency basket, the SDR - which includes the dollar, the yen and other major currencies. 

 The Bank of Latvia engages in passive intevention whenever the lat threatens to break through the limints of its band against the SDR.

title: Latvian c.bank says saw hefty  intervention  in Nov.
text:
RIGA, Dec 12 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Wednesday that during its November interventions on the local currency market it bought foreign exchange worth 70.1 million lats ($112.1 million) to keep the lat within its band. 

 Dealers have said a wide differential between the lat rates and interest on SDR currencies has kept the local unit at the central bank's intervention level since October. 

 "This means that we have made a few but sizeable interventions in November buying up foreign currency worth 70.1 million lats," deputy governor of the central bank Ilmars Rimsevics told a news conference. 

 He also said that so far this year the central bank has purchased foreign exchange worth 88.2 million lats through interventions in the local currency market.

 The Bank of Latvia engages in passive intevention whenever the lat threatens to break through the limits of its band against the SDR.

title: Latvian lat near  intervention , seen easing.
text:
RIGA, Dec 4 (Reuters) - The Latvian lat held steady on Tuesday, but dealers said it was set to weaken by the end of the month as fresh funds enter the market after a eurobond issue in November. 

 At 0850 GMT, the lat was four points off the strongest level the central bank allows it to hit. It traded six points off the intervention level early on Monday. 

 The central bank said it had bought 106.55 million euros ($95.52 million) from the state treasury, which it received from the sale of the seven-year eurobond. 

 Dealers said they expected liquidity to improve as these funds would either be deposited with local commercial banks or with the central bank, which in its turn allots liquidity through its daily repo auctions. 

 "Taking into account that rates are unlikely to rise considerably, that Christmas and the end of the year are approaching, I think that the lat has to weaken," said Vereinsbank forex dealer Andrejs Greivulis. 

 Dealers said it was still difficult to predict a level to which the local unit could ease, but the market is mindful of the fact that it usually slides at the end of the year due to seasonal factors. 

 Improving liquidity is expected to keep local interbank rates in check and possibly narrow the diffirential between the lat rates and interest on SDR currencies. 

 The wide differential has kept the local unit at the central bank's intervention level in recent months. 

Latvia's average overnight rate stood at 5.34/6.03 percent on Monday compared to 6.03/6.63 percent a month ago.

title: Latvia  lat strong after $15.5mln  intervention  last wk.
text:
RIGA, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The Latvian lat held strong on Tuesday and dealers said they expected it to stay at the top of its trading band until December. 

 A central bank official said the Bank of Latvia entered the market last week, buying $15.5 million to keep the lat within its two percent trading band against the SDR basket of world currencies. 

 At 0933 GMT on Tuesday, the lat was dead even with the central bank's strongest intervention level. 

 "It is still near the strongest end of the band and I think it will definitely be there until the end of November," said Leonid Ruderman, head trader with Parex Bank. 

 He said the market expects more demand for lats, against euros, by the finance ministry after the country sold a eurobond of 200 million euro earlier this month. But later on the local currency could slide off the top of the band. 

 "I think in December that the lat may weaken after this selloff (of euros against lats)," Ruderman said. 

 In recent years, December has seen the lat move toward the weaker end of its band due to seasonal pressures. 

 A wide rate differential between the lat and SDR currencies following a string of interest rate cuts by the world's major central banks this year has driven the lat to the top of its band recently, and kept the central bank on the market. 

 "Last week we bought approximately $15.5 million," central bank portfolio manager Andrejs Viks told Reuters. 

 He said that figure was dominated by one deal but that more intervention is likely in the days ahead. 

 "I would say yes there would be something this week or next," he added. 

 On the local forex market, the dollar was 0.6272/77 against the lat, while the central bank's rate was 0.6272/399, where it intervenes to keep the currency within its allowed range.

title: Latvian lat strong, seen headed to  intervention .
text:
RIGA, Oct 9 (Reuters) - The Latvian lat eased slightly within its band against the SDR on Tuesday but was still strong after recent gains and dealers expected it hit intervention this week. 

 At 0915 GMT the lat was five points off its top intervention level - the strongest point it is allowed to reach in its two percent band against the SDR basket. It closed some two to three points off intervention on Monday, dealers said. 

 The lat shot up late last week from around 35 points off intervention, as stronger interest rates in Latvia buoyed the local unit within its trading band. 

 "To keep a long position in lats is fairly attractive right now," said Unibanka dealer Kristaps Strazds. 

 Average offered three-month Latvian interbank rates are currently 6.85 percent, about 400 basis points above levels for the SDR basket, dealers say. 

 The rates are being kept high by a tighter stance by the central bank, which has cut daily liquidity offerings through its repo auctions to about one million lats versus seven million as recently as September 21. 

 "That is why rates are so high in Latvia at the moment," said Strazds. "So mostly banks use Lombard facilities now." 

 "I think it is quite probable that there will be intervention this week," he added. 

 On the local market, the dollar was 0.6146/51 against the lat, while the central bank's rate was 0.6141/265, where it intervenes to keep the currency within its two percent band against the SDR. 

 The lat is pegged at 0.7997 to the IMF's world currency basket, the SDR - which includes the dollar, the yen and other major currencies.

title: Latvian lat seen set for more liquidity squeezes.
text:
RIGA, July 18 (Reuters) - Latvia's money market squeeze may be showing signs of easing but analysts say recent trends show it will be back, keeping funds tight until year-end. 

 Tight funds pushed overnight rates above eight percent at the end of June. These have since climbed down, with one-day RIGIBID/RIGIBOR rates down to 6.45/7.01 percent on Tuesday . 

 Latvia has seen cycles of three to four month liquidity squeezes recently, with overnight rates peaking higher every time since last autumn - from some 6.0 last November and 7.0 percent this February to 8.4 percent at end-June. 

 Analysts say the pattern of recurrent liquidity crunches will repeat itself, although the growth in interest rate peaks may have reached its limit. 

 "If current conditions remain unchanged, rates should not exceed the 7.5 percent level and 8.0 percent on the offer side, as the central bank provides financing via its Lombard loans at 7.5 percent," Ivita Steinberga, head of Treasury at Nordea told Reuters. 

 Analysts have blamed a number of factors for the tight liquidity - large issues of government debt, scant funds offered by the central bank amid a booming economy and a scramble by commercial banks to finance their reserves amid growth in their sector. 

 They say the country's rising budget deficit - up to 1.82 percent of GDP from the 1.68 percent initial plan - is also limiting how much liquidity the central bank can offer through repurchase auctions and other operations. 

 "As long as the central bank keeps its Lombard rates between 5.5-6.5-7.5 percent, lat rates on the interbank market can keep fluctuating between 5.0-8.0 percent each month," said Dainis Barups, head of Capital Markets and Investment Banking with Parex Bank. 

 The lat has been trading in ranges near the strongest levels it is allowed to hit in its SDR band on the forex market amid the money market squeeze. This led the Bank of Latvia to intervene during the last week in June, buying $2.5 million. 

 "We could expect the central bank to be pushed into intervention again sooner or later. We are quoting our longer-term rates with that in mind," said Maris Nelsons, a dealer with Hansabanka. 

 In the short term, this week's auction of a two percent stake in Latvian Gas and one-year Treasury bill sale, worth 12.0 million lats, are unlikley to usher in much more activity. 

 "About the Gas auction, those couple of million lats could only push it a couple of points further closer to the central bank's strongest intervention level, not more. It has been staying between 10-15 points off it in recent days," Janis Paplavskis, a dealer with Parex said. 

 The one-year Treasury bond has been seen by market watchers being partially sold at best. 

 Analysts also said the interbank rate jump is not seen translating into more painful rates for corporate borrowers before autumn. 

 "In sectors growing fast, revenues and volumes should be able to compensate for the rate hike, while the ones which see a lower-than-average expansion could face some problems but not before autumn," said Ansis Grasmanis, vice-president of Unibanka said.

text:

title: Latvian lat hovers nine points off  intervention .
text:
RIGA, June 6 (Reuters) - The Latvian lat hovered nine pips off the top of its band on Friday as dealers watched to see whether sky high rates and a buoyant dollar would push the local unit back into its zone of intervention. 

 The dollar was steady at eight-month highs against the euro and three-month highs against the yen after recent data buoyed confidence in a U.S. economic rebound. 

 A strong dollar usually fuels demand on the local market for lats, which become relatively cheap when the greenback rallies. 

 High local interest rates amid a money market squeeze on funds has also made the lat an attractive buy for strong dollars. 

 Dealers say this will keep the lat in close proximity to its intervention level - the strongest point in its band before the central bank is drawn automatically into the market - until the market receives a fresh injection of funds, probably through intervention. 

 "I guess we should see some good (dollar) amounts flowing into the Bank of Latvia to get fresh lats in circulation, only then. We should see selling into the Bank of Latvia," said Parex Bank forex dealer Kaspars Punenovs. 

 "So far, as I know, a couple million dollars was sold, it's nothing. We reckon it should be 20-30 million at least to stabilise the situation, to get the rates down." 

 At 0908 GMT on the local market, the dollar was 0.6400/05 against the lat, while the central bank's rate was 0.6391/521, where it intervenes to keep the currency within its two percent band against the SDR. 

 This put the lat nine points off its strongest intervention level on the bid side, within recent ranges. 

 The recent money market squeeze led the Bank of Latvia to intervene last week, buying $2.5 million.

text:

title: UPDATE 1-Latvia  central bank  supported lat last week.
text:
RIGA, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Monday it intervened last week for the first time in a year to support the lat and keep it within its trading limits against a currency basket. 

 "We started last week in small amounts. We started on November 28," Andrejs Viks, a portfolio manager at the central bank, told Reuters. 

 Analysts said the lat, which is pegged at 0.7997 to the IMF's SDR world currency basket, was weakened by the repatriation of funds from a bank buyout and year-end cash flows. 

 Viks said the central bank sold $3.5 million as the lat touched the lowest levels permitted in its plus or minus one percent band. It was the first central bank intervention since December 3, 1999. 

 The central bank intervenes occasionally when market rates overshoot its own bid and offer spreads, which represent the strongest and weakest points of the band. 

 The central bank only discusses its interventions on the Monday following any activity on the market. 

 The central bank was forced into a spate of intervention in summer 1999 amid mounting budget deficit worries. 

 The lat has been stronger this year thanks to a tighter fiscal stance by the government. 

 Martins Jaunarajs, short-term liquidity manager at Hansabanka, attributed the lat's weakness to year-end cash flows. "I don't think people are going short because they fear a devaluation or interest rate hikes." 

 He said the market was usually volatile in December following a pre-holiday buying spree by retailers of imported goods and as banks hurried to square positions by the end of the year. 

 This year the market has also been drained of lats by a $54 million buyout of shares in leading bank Unibanka by Sweden's SEB. 

 Dealers said they thought SEB used money market borrowing to handle most of the purchase, which would produce no net inflow of foreign currency, while foreign and some other shareholders have been tempted to chase investments abroad amid a stagnant period for Latvian equities. 

 "There was about 20 million lats ($32 million) that was exchanged into dollars or euro in the last few weeks," said one dealer. "That money will most probably will go to other markets."

title: Latvian 6mo T-bill yields,money mkt rates seen down.
text:
RIGA, May 5 (Reuters) - Latvian government debt yields and money market rates look set to soften further next week in line with the central bank's aim to see lower rates, analysts said on Friday. 

 The market also expects the lat to cede some more of its recent gains. 

 Dealers said stocks lack the impetus to move forward next week after the state failed sell five percent stake in oil terminal Ventspils Nafta  on April 28. 

 On Wednesday the finance ministry will sell two million lats ($3.2 million) of six-month T-bills. Their average yield fell to 5.0 percent on April 26 from 5.79 percent before. 

 "I expected something around 4.5 percent as the Bank of Latvia was intervening (on the secondary market) at about 3.5 percent," said Hansabanka dealer Elmars Priksans. 

 "Definitely banks would speculate on that and try to sell them to the central bank later," he said. 

 Dealers said the money market was still indifferent to political developments, even with parliament expected to vote in a new government being formed by Prime Minister-designate Andris Berzins at 1500 GMT. 

 Analysts said only a decision by Berzins' majority government to depart from the outgoing cabinet's tight fiscal policy could affect market sentiment, which seems unlikely based on the government declaration agreed this week.

 "Money market rates probably will go a bit lower as liquidity on the market is high," said Priksans.

 "I think the trend is for the lat to weaken, but slowly. It looks like banks have more interest to buy foreign currency than sell," said Andrejs Greivulis, a dealer at Vereinsbank Riga.

title: FOCUS-Latvia seals IMF deal, seen boosting lat.
text:
RIGA, Sept 15 (Reuters) - The IMF and Latvia announced on Wednesday an agreement on an economic policy programme, with promises of deficit reduction that analysts said would boost the beleaguered lat currency but may stymie growth. 

 Latvia's Finance Minister Edmunds said IMF approval of the country's policies should convince markets the government had the strength to defend a currency that has been sagging amid budget deficit worries. 

 The deal allows Latvia to tap World Bank structural adjustment loans (SAL) at favourable rates. 

 Analysts agreed the deal should boost investor confidence, but they said the proof would come when the government launched a planned 75 million euro ($77.5 million) bond issue in October. 

 "The main objective of this programme is to lay the foundation for sustained economic growth," IMF representative Adalbert Knobl told a news conference, adding that the IMF sees GDP growth near one percent this year and around four percent next year. 

 "This is to be achieved through two main instruments. The first is to provide for macroeconomic stability through fiscal and monetary restraint that is also supporting the fixed exchange rate of the lat," he said. Structural reform was the second focus. 

 Knobl said the government had agreed to reduce the fiscal deficit from slightly under four percent of GDP this year to under two percent next year, to press ahead with privatisation and boost minority shareholder rights. 

 Improving the regulatory environment, particularly in the energy sector, and banking supervision were also key structural issues to be worked on under the agreement, Knobl added. 

 BORROWING FLEXIBILITY 

 Krastinsh said the IMF programme and stamp of approval gave the government more flexibility in its borrowing plans, and deficit reduction would boost the lat. 

 "What can really put minds at ease is the cutting of budget deficit for 2000 to two percent," Krastinsh said. 

 "The agreement with IMF...will allow us to use the World Bank's structural adjustment loan, pushing any possible borrowing (beyond the October issue) of international markets further down the line. This would happen - if at all necessary - no sooner than before next summer," he said. 

 Analysts said the deficit reduction would strengthen the defence of the lat, which the Bank of Latvia has had to support through sustained foreign exchange market intervention recently. 

 "I think it's important that they have an agreement on the fiscal deficit with an international institution like the IMF," said Erste Bank analyst Petra Frewein. 

 The lat was weak on Wednesday, with dealers saying there were signs of intervention by the central bank after it had been off the market for a week. They said the IMF news would not effect trade drastically in one day. 

 Furthermore, Frewein said the fiscal tightening would not speed recovery for an economy that contracted by 2.3 percent in the first quarter, and the key test of investor confidence would be the October euro bond issue. 

 "I think it will show us if there is a change in the mind of investors... Recently the intervention levels of the central bank have decreased. Perhaps we are moving in a direction where investors are trying to believe in the lat again," Frewein said.

title: FOCUS-Latvia seals IMF deal, lat seen boosted.
text:
RIGA, Sept 15 (Reuters) - The IMF and Latvia announced on Wednesday an agreement on an economic policy programme, with promises of deficit reduction that analysts said would boost the beleaguered lat currency but may stymie growth. 

 Latvia's Finance Minister said IMF approval of the country's policies should convince markets the government had the strength to defend a currency that has been sagging amid budget deficit worries. 

 The deal allows Latvia to tap the World Bank's fund that grants structural adjustment loans (SAL) which makes funds available to countries at favourable rates. 

 Analysts agreed the deal should boost investor confidence, but they said the proof would come when the government launched a planned 75 million euro bond issue in October. 

 FISCAL RESTRAINT, STRUCTURAL REFORM 

 "The main objective of this programme is to lay the foundation for sustained economic growth," IMF representative Adalbert Knobl told a news conference, adding that the IMF sees GDP growth near one percent this year, and around four percent next year. 

 "This is to be achieved through two main instruments, the first is to provide for macroeconomic stability through fiscal and monetary restraint that is also supporting the fixed exchange rate of the lat," he said, adding that structural reform was the second focus. 

 Knobl said the government had agreed to reduce the fiscal deficit from slightly under four percent of GDP this year to under two percent next year, to press ahead with privatisation and boost minority shareholder rights. 

 Improving the regulatory environment, particularly in the energy sector, and banking supervision were also key structural issues to be worked on under the agreement, Knobl added. 

 PROGRAMME GIVES BORROWING FLEXIBILITY 

 Finance Minister Edmunds Krastinsh said the IMF programme and stamp of approval gave the government more flexibility in its borrowing plans, with deficit reduction boosting the lat. 

 "What can really put minds at ease is the cutting of budget deficit for 2000 to two percent," Krastinsh said. 

 "The agreement with IMF...will allow us to use the World Bank's structural adjustment loan, pushing any possible borrowing (beyond the October issue) of international markets further down the line. This would happen - if at all necessary - no sooner than before next summer," he said. 

 Analysts said the deficit reduction would strengthen the defence of the lat, which the Bank of Latvia has had to support through sustained foreign exchange market intervention recently. 

 "I think it's important that they have an agreement on the fiscal deficit with an international institution like the IMF," said Erste Bank analyst Petra Frewein. 

 However, she said the fiscal tightening would not speed recovery for an economy that contracted by 2.3 percent in the first quarter and the key test of investor confidence would be the October euro bond issue. 

 "I think it will show us if there is a change in the mind of investors...recently the intervention levels of the central bank have decreased. Perhaps we are moving in a direction where investors are trying to believe in the lat again," Frewein said.

title: Latvian c.bank says  intervention  eased last week.
text:
RIGA, Sept 14 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Tuesday it had sold just $8 million last week in foreign exchange market intervention to support the lat currency after selling $30 million the week before. 

 "We sold approximately $8 million last week...now actually we have been out of the market for one week already," Andrejs Viks, portfolio manager at the central bank, told Reuters. 

 The central bank began intervening on an almost daily basis in July as the lat slid against the SDR basket amid budget deficit worries. Intermittent bargain hunting for the dollar exacerbated the Latvian currency's weakness. 

 It said on Monday forex reserves fell 5.4 percent in August to 644.3 million lats ($1.103 billion) due to demand for foreign currency and the closing of swap positions. 

Currency demand turned to appetite for the Latvian currency last week as market players moved to take advantage of higher interbank rates brought on by the general lat drain. 

 The lat was off the central bank's intervention levels lat last week and on Monday but seemed to be easing back on Tuesday. 

 At 0931 the market's offered dollar rate was 0.5894 against the lat while the central bank's rate, which is the level at which it intervenes, was 0.5895. 

 The lat is pegged at 0.7997 lats to the SDR, the IMF's world basket currency, and is allowed to fluctuate in a band of one percent either side. 

 The central bank does not usually enter the market when the lat is safely within the band but steps in more or less automatically when it threatens to leave. 

 ((Burton Frierson, Riga newsroom +371 722 2079, reuters@reuters.lv)).
