title: Latvian cbank says Aug  intervention  around $40 mln.
text:
RIGA, Aug 30 (Reuters) - The Bank of Latvia has sold around $40 million while intervening on the local foreign exchange market so far in August, as the lat currency sagged amid worries over the budget deficit, the central bank said on Monday. 

 Arvids Sipols, deputy head of the central bank's forex department, also told Reuters that the bank had intervened on the market on Monday. 

 "Around $40 million for the month. Those are rounded figures and they will of course show up on the balance sheet quarterly reports," Sipols said. 

 "I guess the psychological environment is not so healthy so we've been hitting the market rates, so we are doing something in the market (today)," he added. 

 Sipols said the central had sold about $20 million during interventions last week and $18 million the week before. 

 He declined to comment on the size of intervention on Monday since the bank usually does not discuss how much it buys or sells on a daily basis. 

 At 1239 GMT the market's offered dollar rate was 0.5931 against the lat while the central bank's rate, which is its intervention rate, was 0.5932. 

 The lat has remained weak since last month after the central bank intervened for the first time this year amid currency worries originally sparked by a gaping budget deficit. 

 Parliament earlier this month passed a package of 27.95 million lats worth of spending cuts to the 1999 budget but they were less than half the amount recommended by the central bank. 

 Analysts say the government will have to find more ways to reduce spending this year since the fiscal deficit is expected to reach 3.5 percent of GDP as the budget stands now. 

 Intermittent dollar weakness abroad has further hurt already weak lat sentiment due to bargain hunting for the U.S. currency. 

 Recent local media reports of comments by Ventspils Mayor Aivars Lembergs - who had said he was moving municipal funds into dollars due to lat worries - also hit retail-level sentiment. 

 The lat is pegged at 0.7997 lats to the SDR, the IMF's world basket currency, and is allowed to fluctuate in a band of one percent either side. 

 The central bank does not usually enter the market when the lat is safely within the band but steps in more or less automatically when it threatens to leave.

title: FOCUS- Latvia  sells $40mln in August  intervention .
text:
RIGA, Aug 30 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank entered the forex market to boost the sagging lat currency on Monday, continuing a spate of intervention in which it said it sold $40 million this month amid pension and budget deficit worries. 


At 1350 GMT the market's offered dollar rate	  was 0.5932 against the lat while the central bank's rate, which is its intervention rate, was also 0.5932	 .


 The lat has been weak for the past month since the central bank intervened for the first time this year amid currency worries originally sparked by a gaping budget deficit. This month it said it had sold $40 million during interventions. 

 "Around $40 million for the month. Those are rounded figures and they will of course show up on the balance sheet quarterly reports," said Arvids Sipols, deputy head of the central bank's forex department. 

 "I guess the psychological environment is not so healthy so we've been hitting the market rates, so we are doing something in the market (today)," he added. 

 At the end of July central bank foreign reserves stood at 681.3 million lats, after falling 13.3 million lats that month. 

 Dealers said they were not worried by the size of August's intervention and central bank reserves looked good for now. 

 "If it (the rate of intervention) continued for three, four or five months, that could become a bit dangerous for lat stability...(but) of course the market is waiting for some bigger budget cuts," the dealer added. 

 Earlier this month parliament approved 27.95 million lats in cuts to the 1999 budget, less than half the amount recommended by the central bank. A fiscal deficit of 3.5 percent of GDP is still expected as the budget stands now. 

 Intermittent dollar weakness abroad has further hurt already weak lat sentiment due to bargain hunting for the U.S. currency. 

 Recent comments by Ventspils Mayor Aivars Lembergs - who said he was moving municipal funds into dollars due to lat worries - also hit retail sentiment. 

 Adding further to the lat's problems in recent days has been the issue of pension reform. 

 Parliament earlier this month, along with the 1999 spending cuts, approved pension amendments to shore up next year's budget, but the opposition managed to block implementation. 

 Supporters of a referendum now have until October 5 to collect 134,000 signatures to force a poll which could overturn the deputies' vote. 

 A Latvian finance ministry spokeswoman said on Monday Minister Edmunds Krastinsh believes a failure to cut spending on pensions will threaten the long-term stability of the lat. "He connects this with the overall economic situation in Latvia and problems with the social budget, which may lead to further borrowing that may, later, prompt a devaluation of the lat," spokeswoman Baiba Melnace told Reuters. 

 The lat is pegged at 0.7997 lats to the SDR, the IMF's world basket currency, and is allowed to fluctuate in a band of one percent either side. 

 The central bank does not usually enter the market when the lat is safely within the band but steps in more or less automatically when it threatens to leave.

title: FOCUS-Latvian 7-mo budget deficit 73.89 mln lats.
text:
RIGA, Aug 26 (Reuters) - Latvia said on Thursday the budget deficit continued to rise in July, and dealers expected the news to keep an already weak lat currency soft but did not see it causing major new ripples on the local foreign exchange market. 

 Latvia's consolidated state budget deficit for the first seven months of the year was 73.89 million lats, a rise from 67.281 million lats after the first half of 1999, the finance ministry said in a statement. 

 Finance Minister Edmunds Krastinsh also told a news conference that the first sign of any improvement in tax revenues - which have slumped under the weight of last year's Russian crisis - would appear in October at the earliest. 

 "We will see first in October if the positive signs we have seen in the economy indeed signify a recovery after the Russian crisis," Krastinsh told a news conference. 

 Retail-level worries over the gaping fiscal deficit forced the central bank last month to intervene for the first time this year to support the lat after six-month budget deficit figures were announced. 

 Dealers say it has been on the local forex market on an almost daily basis ever since, although volumes are small and foreign positions have yet to emerge against the lat. 

 Intermittent dollar weakness abroad has further hurt already weak lat sentiment due to bargain hunting for the U.S. unit, but the budget has been the main focus, dealers say. 

 Latvia's budget deficit is expected to reach 3.5 percent of GDP this year, even after a 27.95 million lat package of spending cuts approved by parliament earlier this month. 

 The cuts were less than half what the central bank had recommeded. 

 The World Bank's country director for Poland and the Baltic states, Basil Kavalsky, last week joined a chorus of analysts calling for further cuts, telling Reuters in an interview it was "the key to the stability of the lat". 

 "I think more fiscal tightening is needed," said Leonid Ruderman, head trader at local Parex Bank. 

 However, Ruderman did not expect Thursday's news about the deficit to affect forex trade. 

 "The Bank of Latvia has been (intervening) selling dollars all this week. The lat can't weaken any further," Ruderman said. 

 Analysts say the central bank's reserve position remained strong going into August - despite July's intervention - and the government is still flush with funds after selling a 150 million euro bond in May. 

 "The central bank will not face any additional pressure (due to the budget deficit news)," said Martinsh Jaunarajs, short-term liquidity manager with Hansabana. 

 "This won't create a new wave of dollar buyers but this (negative) sentiment on the retail level will keep on for some time," Jaunarajs added. 

 ((Riga Newsroom +371 722 2079, riga.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: INTERVIEW-World Bank sees budget key to stable lat.
text:
RIGA, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Latvia should take more steps to cut the 1999 fiscal deficit, which will be the key to ensuring the lat currency's stability, the World Bank said on Friday. 

 In an interview with Reuters, the World Bank's country director for Poland and the Baltic states, Basil Kavalsky, also said Latvian 1999 GDP growth would be "almost flat", 2000's two percent and between four and six percent in 2001. 

 Russia's financial crisis last year pushed Latvia into a recession that has put a strangle hold on budget revenues, creating a burgeoning fiscal deficit that has led to retail level worries over the lat's stability. 

 Parliament approved a 27.95 million lat package of budget spending cuts two weeks ago, but they were less than half of what the central bank said should be trimmed and will still leave a fiscal deficit of 3.5 percent of GDP. 

 "There's no doubt that this (deficit) remains somewhat too high in this situation. So there's another round of cuting I'm affraid," Kavalsky said. 

 Last month Latvia's central bank intervened on the local foreign exchange market for the first time this year, selling dollars to support a lat weakened by worries on the retail level that the deficit was undermining the currency. 

 "Some of the steps that the government took in relation to reducing (expenditures) on the pensions were a step in the right direction and I hope those steps would be maintained," Kavalsky said. 

 "But there will have to be additional steps as well. This is, I think, the key to the stability of the lats and to the success of the (IMF) programme." 

 Latvia's memorandum with the IMF ran out in the spring as the government and the fund postponed talks on a new one until a clearer picture of budget revenues emerged. 

 "I think its very critical that the government and IMF reach agreement on such a programme, and we are confident that if agreement can be reached the overall outlook is a positve one," Kavalsky said. 

 Talks on a new memorandum are to begin in September. 

 Latvia's economy contracted by 1.9 percent in the fourth quarter and 2.3 percent in the first three months this year, due to the slump in exports caused by last year's rouble devaluation in Russia, once Latvia's mainstay market. 

 Kavalsky said 1999 GDP would be almost flat or see "perhaps a very small decline" but that signs of improvement in Russia and Western Europe gave reason for optimism beyond that. 

 Latvia's central bank has forecast 1999 GDP growth at between one and two percent 

 "Next year the growth rate will still be modest but I think there is potential on the up side of that forecast actually," Kavalsky said. 

 Along with Russia's decline, analysts say sluggishness in Western Europe has hurt efforts of companies to redirect sales there. 

 "Clearly the situation in Russia has bottomed out, and there is some expansion in the Russian economy," Kavalsky said. 

 "The European economies are looking much more promising in the year ahead and both those are very positive signs for the Latvian economy and trade here in Latvia." 

 ((Riga Newsroom +371 722 2079, riga.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS-Latvian c.bank wants 1999 deficit lowered.
text:
RIGA, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank on Wednesday urged the government to take steps to limit the 1999 fiscal deficit but said the lat currency faced no devaluation threat, despite its recent weakness caused by budget woes. 

 Parliament last week passed a 27.95 million lat ($47.25 million) package of spending cuts to the 1999 budget. The cuts were half what the central bank had said were needed and will still leave the budget with a deficit of 3.5 percent of planned 1999 GDP. 

 "The central bank would urge the government to make any necessary steps to reduce the fiscal deficit below three percent (of GDP) this year," Bank of Latvia President Einars Repshe told a news conference. 

 Finance Minister Edmunds Krastinsh told Reuters the central bank's fiscal deficit target was possible but depended on a recovery in tax revenues in the second half. 

 "If the economy picks up and revenues improve, it is possible. To come to three percent we would need to generate additional 20 million lats or so during the remaining five months," Krastinsh said. 

 Budget deficit worries, mostly on the retail level, forced the central bank to intervene for the first time this year on the local foreign exchange market last month as the lat weakened against the SDR world currency basket it is pegged to. 

 In recent days dealers have seen more signs of intervention as a weak dollar abroad fed fresh demand for the U.S. unit and then concerns over Russia's political situation further weakened lat sentiment. It was again soft on Wednesday. 

 "Dollar/lat is at the intervention band. It's been hovering there all day so probably the Bank of Latvia is in the market (intervening)," said one dealer. 

 However, Repshe said there was no threat of devaluation and that the central bank could defend it if necessary. 

 "There is no devaluation risk and it will not be allowed, either now or in the foreseeable future. The central bank has both the political will and sufficient resources to do that, with lat coverage at 114 percent," Repshe said. 

 Analysts said markets took last week's cuts as a sign of more to come and would be disappointed if the government did not tighten further. 

 "To (stabilise) the market and to take pressure off the currency then it would be wise to adjust these spending cuts a little bit more," said Raymond Beimers, an economist with ABN Amro. 

 "Being such a small country with a lot of other imbalances it would be wise to have the deficit at (most) at three percent of GDP but even less would be better," said Beimers. 

 Latvia's economy was pushed into a recession after the Russian rouble devaluation last August cut it off from its mainstay market, squeezing tax revenues and forcing the government into budget cuts. 

 ((Riga Newsroom +371 722 2079, reuters@reuters.lv)) ($1=.5915 Latvian Lat).

title: Baltic sentiment seen weaker on Russia turmoil.
text:
VILNIUS, Aug 9 (Reuters) - Russia's latest political upheaval may further weaken poor market sentiment in its Baltic neighbours, although their currencies face no immediate threat, analysts said on Monday. 

 "The events in Russia do not add to the picture of stability. They clearly show that the crisis in Russia has not ended, as some analysts had said," said Hermis Finance chief analyst Nerijus Dagilis after Russian President Boris Yeltsin sacked his prime miniser. 

 Yeltsin sacked Sergei Stepashin and appointed Security Council chief Vladimir Putin as acting premier, saying he wanted Putin to succeed him in the presidency. 

 The rouble weakened and Moscow shares fell on the surprise announcement of Russia's fifth new acting premier in 17 months. 

 But Baltic equity markets, like other international markets, took the news in their stride and ended mixed with no sharp movements in share indices and forex markets fairly quiet. 

 Analysts said the currencies of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which came under pressure following last August's financial crisis in Moscow, had felt no speculative attacks. 

 "Most banks have minimum exposure to Russia so it is really a matter of how the Baltic currencies are seen. Right now activity has not picked up," said Estonian Hansapank money trader Maivi Hanson. 

 Dealers said the news was likely to hit Latvia's lat hardest since it has spent much of recent weeks stuck at the bottom of its one percent fluctuation band against the IMF's SDR world currency basket. 

 Budget worries and then a weak dollar have spurred local demand for the greenback, causing a spate of intervention by Latvia's central bank in recent weeks. 

 "For the lat this, of course, is not good news," said one Latvian forex trader. 

 In Lithuania, where the litas is pegged at four to one dollar, analysts said there was greater concern that the government could press for a devaluation to boost growth than of a speculative attack causing a break to the peg. 


Equities ended little changed, with Estonia's TALSE	   index down 0.15 percent, Latvia's RICI	   off 0.79 percent and Lithuania's Litin-10		up 0.3 percent.



"Investors have already discounted Russia into prices. Instability is the normal situation there," said Optiva Pank equity dealer Kaur Elviste.



Baltic share markets, which have been punished by recurring Russian and emerging markets crises in the past two years, are not seen having room to fall much further. But the reshuffle could postpone indefinitely the return of foreign investors.

title: Latvian dealers see signs of c.bank  intervention .
text:
RIGA, Aug 6 (Reuters) - Latvian dealers said on Friday they saw more signs of central bank intervention on the local foreign exchange market as a weak dollar abroad and budget worries continued to feed dollar demand. 

 "I think the Bank of Latvia intervened today," said one dealer. 

 "It's quite active today and there have been some sellers of dollars, which haven't been around for two days, but the situation is the same as yesterday - dollar/lat is at intervention," the dealer added. 

 At 1205 GMT the market's offered dollar rate was 0.5908 against the lat and the central bank's rate, which is its intervention level, was 0.5909. 

 The central bank no longer comments daily on whether it intervenes. 

 Last month saw a spate of intervention amid worries, mostly on the retail level, that the country's gaping budget deficit could undermine the lat currency's stability. 

 Dealers said it intervened on Wednesday and Thursday and that deficit worries had been revived after opposition MPs managed to postpone the implementation of amendments to the pension law aimed at bolstering next year's budget. 

 Latvia's parliament on Thursday approved a package of 27.95 million lats ($47 million) in cuts to the 1999 state budget, which was less than originally planned. 

 The lat is pegged at 0.7997 lats to the SDR, the IMF's world basket currency, and is allowed to fluctuate in a band of one percent either side. 

 The central bank does not generally intervene while the lat remains safely within its corridor, but steps in more or less automatically when it threatens to leave its fluctuation band. 

 The central bank's offered rates represent the widest points in the band.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Baltics feel the  currency  strain.
text:
LONDON, Aug 3 (Reuters) - Baltic currency pegs have the technical strength to withstand recent devaluation pressures, foreign analysts say, but the question is whether governments are prepared to take the pain of maintaining them. 

 While few doubt Estonia's commitment to its currency board system, analysts say Lithuania's currency peg looks vulnerable to political adjustment, and Latvia's could follow suit. 

 "None of them will be forced into devaluation - they've got enough reserves," said Tim Ash, emerging Europe economist at Westdeutsche Landesbank in London. 

 "But there is a real risk, particularly in Lithuania, that the government will decide the price of defending the peg by tightening fiscal policy is too much for the economy to bear." 

 Lithuanian central bank head Reinoldijus Sharkinas has long insisted that devaluing the litas from its current four-to-one dollar peg is out of the question. 

 Latvia's central bank and Finance Ministry have both said they see no devaluation threat to the lat, which trades in a band of plus or minus one percent around the International Monetary Fund's SDR basket currency, as long as the government sticks to tough spending cuts this year. 

 Estonia's currency board system, which pegs the kroon at 15.6466 to the euro, is enshrined in the country's constitution. 

 But recession and big current-account deficits have weighed heavily on Baltic markets since Russia's financial crisis last year hit exports from the three former Soviet states, and a round of regional devaluations sapped their competitiveness. 

 Worst hit are Lithuania and Latvia, which have not forged the close Scandinavian links that have buoyed the Estonian economy since independence in 1991. 

 Lithuania's current-account gap rose to a huge 12.1 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) last year, and to 9.6 percent in the first quarter of 1999. Latvia's was scarcely better, rising to 11 percent last year and 8.7 percent in the first quarter. 

 In contrast, Estonia's current-account deficit shrank to 8.6 percent of GDP last year, and 7.0 percent in the first quarter. 

 Speculation rumbles on that Lithuania may take advantage of its planned switch from a dollar to a currency basket peg, probably next year, to haul down the value of the litas, and analysts say the uncertainty is undermining equity prices. 

 Rating agency Fitch IBCA recently voiced "increasing concern about the appropriateness of the current level" of the litas. 

 In Latvia, the central bank recently had to intervene five days running to keep the lat within its trading band. 

 "Basically you have to look at the resolve on the part of politicians to hold the line, and in Lithuania it's weakest," Ash at WestLB said. 

 The dollar's relentless rise for most of this year against the euro has piled on the pain for Lithuania, while easing pressure on Estonia and leaving the lat largely untouched. 

 But analysts said the euro's recent upturn against the greenback offered Lithuania only limited relief. 

 "It gives them a bit more room, but fundamentally it doesn't change the current-account deficit," said Juliet Sampson, emerging market currency strategist at Bank of America. 

 "They haven't reached breaking point, but that doesn't mean they won't choose to go." 

 Devaluation for one Baltic currency would inevitably have a knock-on effect on the others, and could rattle other currency pegs even further afield. 

 "If one goes it'll put a strain on all the others," Sampson said. "For that matter, if one goes it'll put a strain on Hong Kong to some extent." ((London Capital Markets +44 171 542 6414, fax 583 7239, gill.tudor@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS-Latvian  central bank intervenes  again.
text:
RIGA, July 23 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank on Friday intervened for the fourth day in a row to support the lat, which remained weak amid budget deficit worries despite government plans for large spending cuts to bolster the currency. 

 However, analysts said the lat was not in imminent danger of devaluation. They expected finance ministry plans for about 50 million lats ($84 million) in spending cuts in the 1999 budget eventually to reassure the market. 

Central bank foreign exchange dealer Karlis Bauze told Reuters the Bank of Latvia had again intervened on Friday to keep the lat in its corridor after entering the market for the first time this year on Tuesday. 

 "Yes, we did (enter the market)...We did one small operation but it was very light." 

 The lat is pegged at 0.7997 lats to the SDR, the IMF's world basket currency, and is allowed to fluctuate in a band of one percent either side. 

 The central bank does not generally intervene while the lat remains safely within its corridor, but steps in more or less automatically when it threatens to leave its fluctuation band. 

 Finance Minister Edmunds Krastinsh told Latvian Radio that the government was eying some 50 million lats in spending cuts which would "affect almost all branches". 

 He said the 1999 budget deficit would be between three and five percent of GDP, depending on privatisation revenue. 

 The new government, which took over last week after the previous one resigned amid criticism of its handling of the budget, has pledged to cut the deficit to shore up the lat's economic fundamentals. 

 Krastinsh also said Latvia expected to tap international debt markets next year, and would base its 2000 budget conservatively on expectations of 3.5 percent GDP growth and 3.0 percent inflation. 

 Analysts said it remained to be seen whether the government would have to cut more than 50 million lats in expenditure. 

 "In this turbulent situation I'd say this was quite a good introductory step and perhaps the government will follow with even more if the markets push them to do so...(but) the absolute levels of borrowing are relatively low even compared to some emerging markets," said Hansabank Markets analyst Urmas Riel. 

 "At least the trend should be well received by the markets." 

 But dealers said it would take time for the news to bolster the lat. 

 "Generally (lat intervention) is not over yet, but of course the amounts are small, it's mainly local market demand, no international demand," said Janis Strazinskis, senior foreign exchange dealer with Vereinsbank.

The central bank does not intervene actively to support the lat, but it acts as a supplier of last resort when market rates overshoot either side of the fluctuation band. 

 It does not disclose the levels at which it intervenes but its offered rates represent the widest points in the band. 

 The central bank, which intervened last year amid worries over the Russian crisis, was forced to support the lat due to the market's concerns over the poor economy and a gaping budget deficit. 

 Pro-business Prime Minister Andris Shkele, who took over last week after his predecessor Vilis Krishtopans resigned amid sharp criticism over his handling of the budget, has pledged budget cuts to shore up the lat's economic foundations. 

 "They seem to be very concerned about the budget and it looks like they are determined to do something about it... I don't see them devaluing," said Deutsche Bank analyst Chris Blevins. 

 "If they devalued imports would become much more expensive and Latvia is in the transition period where they're updating infrastructure, industrial complex and so-forth, therefore devaluing would very much hurt that effort," Blevins added. 

 Devaluation could also lead to painful central bank rate hikes to combat inflation, which is currently subdued. 

 Analysts also said the government would put itself in a bigger bind by devaluing, which would raise the cost of servicing foreign debt such as a 150 million euro ($156.9 million) bond it launched in May. 

 However, other analysts said the market may have already decided that Latvia's economy will not mend itself without a devaluation to revive exports to Russia, once its mainstay market until it dried up last year after the rouble devaluation. 

 "I don't think necessarily it has to happen but on the other hand if (devaluation) did happen it would not be really surprising," said Handelsbanken analyst Gunnar Tersman. 

 "It would be a natural reaction to the situation they are in with a weak economy...and budget problems and all of these things, all of them related to the Russian crisis." 

 ($1=.9557 Euro).

title: FOCUS-Latvian cbank  intervenes  to support weak lat.
text:
RIGA, July 20 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank entered the forex market for the first time this year on Tuesday as the lat sagged and analysts said the new government needed to act quickly on a gaping budget deficit to shore up the currency. 

 The dollar opened at 0.6020 to the lat, continuing a soft trend before the central bank intervened at 0.6012, dealers said. At 1235 GMT the offered dollar rate was 0.6007 against the lat. 

 "Yes, we did (enter the market)...but this is passive intervention. This means that it is much cheaper for banks to buy dollars from us, not other banks," Bank of Latvia forex dealer Karlis Bauze told Reuters. 

 Latvia's central bank does not enter the market actively to support the lat, which is pegged to the SDR basket of world currencies at 0.7997 and fluctuates against it in a plus/minus one percent band. 

 It does regularly offer rates at the end of the fluctuation band as a last resort for banks. Last August, the central bank intervened on the market to support the lat during the Russian financial crisis. 

 Dealers said it was the first time this year the Bank of Latvia had entered the market and blamed worries over the budget deficit and an economic slump. 

 The central bank would not say at what level banks began selling them lats. 

 "Mainly I think it is the bad macroeconomic situation and the bad situation with the budget," said Martinsh Strazds, a dealer with Unibanka, although he said dollar demand was not aggressive and trade was slow. 

 Latvia's economy contracted by 2.3 percent in the first quarter after shrinking by 1.9 percent in the last three months of 1998 due to the effects of Russia's crisis. 

 Analysts say there is little the government can do to stimulate growth until the Russian export market, the mainstay of Latvian producers until last year's rouble devaluation, recovers or Western Europe sees a growth spurt. 

 It can cut the budget deficit, which widened to 47.5 million lats from a 29.2 million lat shortfall at the end of May. The last government was seen struggling to keep it under three percent of GDP to keep Latvia's EU hopes alive. 

 "If they really want to avoid a devaluation...they have to demonstrate to the markets that they are serious in keeping their economy in balance and that would necessitate budget cuts and it would also require that authorities can accept higher unemployment," said Handelsbanken analyst Gunnar Tersman. 

 New Prime Minister Andris Shkele, who took over last week after Vilis Krishtopans resigned amid sharp criticism over his handling of the economy, has said the top priority of his cabinet would be to begin putting the state's finances back in order. 

 ((Riga Newsroom +371 722 2079, reuters@reuters.lv)).

title: C.bank sees lats stable, confirms  intervene .
text:
RIGA, Aug 28 (Reuters) - Latvia's central bank said on Friday the stability of the lat currency was not threatened by Latvian banks' exposure to Russian debt. 

 But in a news conference, central bank president Einars Repshe said the Bank of Latvia had intervened recently. 

 "We have sold small dollar sums in recent days," Repshe said. 

 "Lats stability is in no way threatened and I would suggest people who do not need dollars should wait with buying. It will simply be cheaper when the demand falls," Repshe said. 

 The bank said it had ample resources to support the currency, which is pegged to the SDR - a special monetary unit of the International Monetary Fund made up of major world currencies - and is 100 percent backed by reserves. 

 "In a couple days or weeks lats will return to the lower border of the intervention band," he added. 

 ((Riga newsroom +371 722 2079, riga.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: LATVIAN O/N RATES CLIMB, DOLLAR UP VS LAT.
text:
RIGA, Sept 23 (Reuter) - Latvian overnight rates climbed on Tuesday and were seen rising further as banks borrow to meet their monthly reserve requirments, dealers said. 

 In forex markets, the dollar jumped late Monday on a surge of strong demand but brokers could not say who was behind the deals or why. 

 Overnight rates rose on Tuesday to a bid/ask range of 2.30/3.00 percent from 2.0 to 2.50 percent after hardly moving last week. 

 "There is a lot more activity on the market this week and the rates should continue to climb," said Maris Vinklers of Hansabank Markets' interest rate products department. 

 He added that banks were now borrowing to meet the reserve requirements of the central bank. 

 In the foreign exchange markets, a late Monday order pushed the dollar up against the lat. 

 The lat eased against the dollar late Monday to 0.5846/51 from 0.5825/35 and held steady there on Tuesday morning. The Bank of Latvia intervention rate was 0.5824. 

 Dealers were at a loss to explain the sudden order for dollars but said morning trade was quiet. 

 "Activity is down this morning," said Andris Savickis, a dealer with Rigas komercbanka. 

 -- Ed Stoddard, Riga newsroom +371 721 52 40

title: LATVIA-O/N RATES STEADY, LAT IN DEMAND.
text:
RIGA, Sept 19 (Reuter) - Latvian overnight rates remained steady on Friday but dealers expected them to edge up next week when banks scramble to meet their end of the month reserve requirements. 

 On the the foreign exchange markets, increased stock market activity was seen driving demand for the lat but it eased against the dollar, which rose sharply on global markets on Thursday night, dealers said. 

 Overnight rates were virtually unchanged at a bid ask range of 1.70/2.50. 

 "Things have been very quiet all week and rates have hardly changed a notch," said Maris Vinklers of Hansabank-Latvija's money market's department. 

 "The market should be more active next week when banks try to make their reserve requirements for the central bank," he said. 

 The local forex market was relatively busy as investors playing the reinvigorated bourse snapped up lats. 

 Latvian shares eased this week but trade volumes remained high. 

 "There is a big demand for lats now which is linked to the rally on the stock market," said one dealer. 

 But the dollar's overnight surge knocked the lat down a bit. 

 The lat/dollar rate eased to the Bank of Latvia's intervention rate of 0.5816/20 on Friday morning from Thursday's close of 0.5805/15. 

 -- Ed Stoddard, Riga newsroom +371 721 52 40

title: LATVIA-O/N RATES UP AHEAD OF WEEKEND, LAT SEEN EASING.
text:
RIGA, July 11 (Reuter) - Overnight rates rose ahead of the weekend and the lat/dollar rate came close to the Bank of Latvia's intervention rate on Friday. 

 But dealers said that the lat was expected to ease slightly in response to local market demand for dollars. 

 Volumes on both markets were relatively low because of the summer holiday, dealer said. 

 Overnight rates climbed to a bid/ask of 4.00/4.50 percent on Friday from 3.20/4.20 percent on Thursday. 

 Dealers said rates usually rise ahead of the weekend as banks have three days to meet their reserve requirements and expected them to fall next week. 

 In foreign exchange markets, the interbank lat/dollar rate was steady at 0.5699/704, near the central bank's intervention rate of 0.5696/811. 

 "This situation won't last as we don't expect banks to sell dollars to the central bank...There is a big order for dollars from a couple of sources right now," said one dealer. 

 Dealers declined to name the source. 

 -- Ed Stoddard, Riga newsroom +371 721 52 40

title: LATVIAN OVERNIGHT RATES STAY LOW, DEALERS EYE EU SUMMIT.
text:
RIGA, June 16 (Reuter) - Overnight rates remained low in Latvia as the liquidity situation in the banks remained healthy, dealers said on Monday. 

 Dealers said that overnight rates were at the same levels as Friday's 1.75 percent to 2.75 percent. 

 "There are more lenders than borrowers right now...banks do not seem concerned about their liquidity situation and their obligations to the central bank," said Maris Vinklers, head of money markets at Hansabank-Latvija. 

 He added that rates were expected to remain low for the rest of the month. 

 The lat was trading against the dollar near the Bank of Latvia's intervention rate of 0.5706 in a range of 0.5709 to 0.5713, almost the same level as Friday. 

 "There are a lot of investments coming into Latvia now, and so there is a big demand for lats," said one dealer. 

 "The dollar could gain against the lat, depending on the outcome of the EU summit in Amsterdam and its impact on European currencies," the dealer added. 

 -- Ed Stoddard, Riga newsroom +371 721 52 40

title: Exotic  Currency /Latvia -2: Pegged To SDR Basket
text:
Since February 1994, the lat has formally been pegged to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) Special Drawing Rights (SDR) currency basket. This means the lat exchange rate changes only when other currencies in the the SDR basket fluctuate. One SDR is equal to 0.7997 lats. 

 On Wednesday, one U.S. dollar was worth 0.547 lats, a rate unchanged for nearly a year, except for the period when the U.S. dollar weakened against the SDR last spring. 

 Even during the height of the banking crisis in 1995, the lat held against the SDR, sparing the central bank, the Bank of Latvia, from having to intervene. 

 Though the currency remained unscathed, the banking crisis has damaged investor confidence in the country, widened an already widening budget deficit and dashed expectations of economic growth. 

 And while this legacy leaves the currency stable, it doesn't spell a great deal of investor confidence in the country. 

 "It's a bad memory that will inhibit things," said Viksnins, referring to the lingering effects of the banking crisis. "I certainly wouldn't put $1,000 in a bank in Latvia." 

 According to a report on Latvia by Union Bank of Switzerland, the country lags Estonia in attracting foreign capital. The blame for this is divided between the slow pace of privatization and lingering doubts about the banking system. 

 Viksnins, however, emphasizes that the banking crisis had unforeseen currency benefits as it curbed speculative capital that could have entered the country to take advantage of the central bank's anti-inflationary, high interest rates.
